## Transcript

[Outtakes] Uh, bleugh. It's a Teletubby, sorry can I say that again?
Guillermo Rauch. I'm Lee. I'm Jared Palmer. I'm Delba de Oliveira. I'm Lydia Hallie.
What is Vercel? My first thought when when I was starting a company was how do I create a top-notch
website that's really fast and uses the latest technologies, but I felt like I needed to take
a PhD just putting the compilers and tools and infrastructure together and I just want to create
a website really quickly to share my ideas with the world, and when I found out that it was so hard
and so challenging, I decided to create a platform so that no one would have that problem again.
What cliche programming word do you overuse? Orthogonal. Lately I've been using mental
model. Abstraction, indirection. Oof so many. Layers of indirection, ooh orthogonal.
Orthogonal, as well for sure totally overused across the industry. Blazing fast
What is your favorite meme? Oh I make my own memes, but they're too sassy to share. Anything
from Jared Palmer's Twitter account. I like Obama congratulating himself that one's good
Uh you versus the guy she tells you not to worry about, that one's good too.
Why build on the Web? I think the web is a platform for freedom, first and foremost. I
think there are other great platforms out there, but none like the web in the ability to empower
everybody in the world to connect and distribute information through hyperlinks. Because the web
is ours, it belongs to all of us, it is one of Humanity's greatest inventions and we are its
stewards and that is something that we should take seriously. It's the world's most open platform,
it has an unparalleled deployment model.
You can push a change and have it be live on the next request. With the web you just have
great SEO, you can build a product and you can instantly reach millions of people
if it becomes successful, because everyone has access to the web, which is amazing.
What makes a great developer experience? I think in addition to having great defaults minimizing
latency so that the user retains their focus. We tend to, at least for speaking for myself, as an
engineer losing focus can be detrimental to your company your team, so I like to invest in things
that give me a great feedback loop with very low latency. Minimal latency between keystrokes
and feedback, error messages that incrementally take you towards the solution. A great developer
experience makes it as easy as possible to get started, but not only thinks about the happy path
also when things go wrong. Feeling like you can iterate fast, easy to debug, good documentation
very important, yeah that's about it. When I go to a web page for a tool or a library and
I know exactly what they do, you'd be surprised how many tools out there don't really tell you
what they actually do. I think great developer experience is a servant to great user experience
and so for me a great developer experience is something that means the the right thing
and the easy thing is the same thing so things like progressive enhancement and accessibility
being defaults for the tools that I'm using, performance optimizations being out of the box,
end-to-end type safety so that I don't ship bugs to production and if I do make a mistake, errors
that guide me towards a solution–these are all the tenets of a good developer experience in my book.
What is your favorite color? Black. The hex code is zero zero zero zero zero zero.
Dogs or cats? Dogs. cats. cats, I have two. dogs. smart dogs or orange cats.
Tailwind or CSS Modules? Tailwind. Tailwind. Tailwind. Tailwind. Neither. Tailwind.
Postgres or MySQL? Postgres. Postgres. Both. Postgres. Postgres. Mongo.
Spaces or tabs? Spaces, or sometimes I change my mind, but mostly spaces. Whatever Prettier does.
Tabs. Whatever Prettier does. Tabs. Tabs come on. Neovim or VSCode? Neovim, for sure.
VSCode. VSCode. VSCode. VSCode. VSCode. New York or San Francisco? San Francisco, not even close.
New York, or nowhere. Iowa, no I'm just kidding, San Francisco. New York. New York. London.
Light mode or dark mode? System, so variable dynamic. System. Dark mode, except when coding
on a beach, or near pool in the sun. Dark mode. Light mode for my body, dark mode for my soul.
Coffee or tea? coffee. coffee. coffee. coffee.
Both. coffee. coffee in the morning tea in the afternoon.
Remote or in person? in person. both. Oh remote,
yeah. Remote. Both. I like people, but I also really like being at home, remote.
How will AI change your job as a developer?
I think AI emphasizes this need for focusing on products first because AI technologies are
very quickly becoming democratized. AI used to be something that was really hard to accomplish as a
company. You needed a lot of machine learning experts and all kinds of ML operations folks.
Nowadays you have all these open APIs that run incredible reasoning machines at scale,
so your opportunity now is to integrate those and present those to customers and consumers.
Anything I say in answer to this question is going to be hilariously out of date 12
months from now but I would guess that based on the experiences that I've had
with AI so far it's gonna enable me to move a lot quicker as a developer AI is
gonna find my mistakes for me and it's going to open pull requests and it's
just going to do all of the drudge work that I currently can't be bothered to do.
What's your favorite emoji? Right now it's fire on fire. it's literally our Slack has a
fire that's on fire so when something's really good it's Fire and Fire. Dead,
it's a Teletubby dramatically fainting. I think my favorite emoji is probably Elmo
fire. This emoji is great because half of the people who see it think that it's a bad thing,
and half of them think it's a good thing, either Elmo is like mad that he's on fire, or it's like
a celebration that everything's on fire and good for me it's a good thing, it's like a happy emoji.
Okay awesome awesome all right thank you [Closing]

In this episode, Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch goes deep on how V0, their text-to-app platform, has already generated over 100 million applications and doubled Vercel’s user base in under a year.

Guillermo reveals how a tiny SWAT team inside Vercel built V0 from scratch, why “vibe coding” is making software creation accessible to everyone (not just engineers), and how the AI Cloud is automating DevOps, making cloud infrastructure self-healing, and letting companies expose their data to AI agents in just five lines of code.

You’ll hear why “every company will have to rethink itself as a token factory,” how Vercel’s Next.js went from a conference joke to powering Walmart, Nike, and Midjourney, and why the next billion app creators might not write a single line of code. Guillermo breaks down the difference between vibe coding and agentic engineering, shares wild stories of users building apps from napkin sketches, and explains how Vercel is infusing “taste” and best practices directly into their AI models.

We also dig into the business side: how Vercel’s AI-powered products are driving explosive growth, why retention and margins are strong, and how the company is adapting to a new wave of non-technical users. In this episode of _The Eric Ries Show_, I’m joined by Guillermo Rauch, CEO and founder of Vercel—a company powering the front end of the internet for brands like OpenAI, Nintendo, Chick-fil-A, and many more. Guillermo’s journey began far from Silicon Valley, in Argentina, where a Red Hat Linux CD changed the course of his life.

We talk about how open source gave him a way in—and why he still believes it’s the ultimate growth engine for companies and careers. Guillermo shares what he learned from building developer tools used by millions, and how Vercel became the go-to platform for the AI era.

In our conversation today, we talk about the following topics:

• How open source paved the way for Guillermo’s career

• The case for open source as a growth strategy

• What makes Silicon Valley special, and how online communities can unlock similar opportunities

• The gap between how elite companies ship software and how most others do

• How Vercel became the go-to for AI startups

• The future of the web: agents, AI clouds, and software 2.0

• Guillermo’s take on vibe coding and why it’s more than just prompts to code

• How recursive founder mode helps Vercel stay fast while scaling

• The challenge of keeping Vercel open, fair, and resistant to abuse

•  And much more!

Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch announced the company's readiness for an IPO, highlighting significant growth driven by AI-generated applications. Speaking at the HumanX conference in San Francisco, Rauch noted that Vercel's annualized revenue surged from $100 million in early 2024 to $340 million by February 2026. This growth is largely attributed to the rise of AI agents, with 30% of applications on Vercel's platform now originating from AI deployments.

Vercel, which completed a $300 million Series F funding round in September 2025, reaching a $9.3 billion valuation, competes with Cloudflare and AWS in hosting services. Despite a generally frozen tech IPO market, Rauch's statement underscores Vercel's confidence in its market position and the expanding infrastructure market. He emphasized that AI is democratizing application development, positioning Vercel as a key player in providing a "home" for this software.
